correct_citation: Kraft, M. A., Schueler, B. E., & Falken, G. T. (2024). What Impacts Should We Expect from Tutoring at Scale? Exploring Meta-Analytic Generalizability. EdWorkingPaper No. 24-1031, Annenberg Institute at Brown University. https://doi.org/10.26300/zygj-m525
design: Meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
population_location: 265 RCTs (340 interventions) published 1967-2023; K-12 students in OECD countries (about 51 studies international/OECD, rest U.S.)
outcome: Standardized math or reading test scores
effect_as_reported: Full-sample pooled effect 0.42 SD; restricted (large-scale U.S., third-party standardized tests) estimates a third to a half as large: 0.21 SD for programs serving 400-999 students, 0.16 SD for 1,000+
excerpt: We conduct an expanded meta-analysis of 265 randomized controlled trials [...] Pooled effect sizes from studies with stronger target-equivalence remain meaningful but are only a third to a half as large as those from our full sample.
note: Count is 265 RCTs; 282 is not a sample count in this paper (likely a stray number). Sample is K-12 in OECD countries, not 'US PreK-12' (inclusion criteria: K-12 students, OECD country). The one-third-to-one-half finding itself is stated as claimed.

correct_citation: McCombs, J. S., Augustine, C. H., Pane, J. F., & Schweig, J. (2020). Every Summer Counts: A Longitudinal Analysis of Outcomes from the National Summer Learning Project. RAND Corporation, RR-3201-WF. (Earlier: Augustine et al. 2016, Learning from Summer, RAND.)
design: Randomized controlled trial (lottery-like random assignment of applicants), plus correlational analyses of attenders
population_location: 5,639 low-income third-grade applicants (spring 2013) in Boston, Dallas, Duval County, Pittsburgh and Rochester; followed to end of grade 7 (spring 2017)
outcome: Fall study-administered math and ELA tests; state assessments; SEL; attendance; behavior
effect_as_reported: ITT 0.08 SD in math in fall 2013 (study-administered assessment), not significant by spring 2014 and none significant after second summer; correlational: high attenders (20+ days) 0.13 math fall 2013, 0.07 spring 2014 state math; after second summer 0.14 math, 0.09 ELA on spring 2015 state tests; by spring 2017 not significant (0.07 math, 0.04 ELA for two-summer high attenders)
excerpt: students in the treatment group outperformed students in the control group by an estimated effect size of 0.08 in mathematics [...] a minimum of about 25 hours of summer mathematics instruction or 34 hours of summer language arts instruction each year
note: Sample is about 5,600 (5,639 applicants), entering grade 4 (completed grade 3), followed through grade 7, not 'grades 3-7' sample of 6,000. The 0.08 ITT was on a fall study-administered test and did not persist. Time-on-task threshold is 25 hours math OR 34 hours ELA each year (not 'and', not only second summer). High-attender advantages were on spring 2015 state tests; they shrank and were non-significant by spring 2017.

correct_citation: Rogers, T., & Feller, A. (2018). Reducing student absences at scale by targeting parents' misbeliefs. Nature Human Behaviour, 2, 335-342. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-018-0328-1

population_location: Parents of 28,080 high-risk K-12 students, School District of Philadelphia (203 schools), 2014-15
outcome: Total absences; chronic absenteeism
effect_as_reported: Most effective versions reduced chronic absenteeism by 10% or more (Nature). Best arm (peer comparison) per Education Next: total absences -6%, chronic absence -11%; WWC means 15.93 vs 17.04 absences, 31.9% vs 36.0% chronically absent. Cost $6.60 per household (Berkeley).
excerpt: Parents of 28,080 high-risk students in grades kindergarten to 12th grade received one of three personalized information treatments repeatedly throughout the school year [...] The most effective versions reduced chronic absenteeism by 10% or more
note: Discrepancies resolved: Philadelphia is confirmed (Berkeley release, WWC: 203 SDP schools). 28,080 is the randomized study sample; WWC's 14,002 is the analytic sample for one treatment-vs-control contrast (grades 1-12); Education Next's '40,300+' is not supported by the paper. '10% or more' (paper) and '6% total / 11% chronic' (Education Next, peer-comparison arm) agree. The claim's WWC statement is wrong: the WWC rates all three arms as meeting standards without reservations (Tier 1).

correct_citation: Gottfried, M. A. (2010). Evaluating the Relationship between Student Attendance and Achievement in Urban Elementary and Middle Schools: An Instrumental Variables Approach. American Educational Research Journal, 47(2), 434-465. https://doi.org/10.3102/0002831209350494

correct_citation: Sala, G., & Gobet, F. (2020). Cognitive and academic benefits of music training with children: A multilevel meta-analysis. Memory & Cognition, 48(8), 1429-1441. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13421-020-01060-2
